cards.text: We're near the end of a love song, friend, where two lovers have spent the whole song praising each other. Now a voice asks who this is, coming up and leaning on her beloved. The only thing I ever leaned on was a pile of takeout menus in a junk drawer.

cards.question: She's coming up, leaning on her beloved. Where is she coming up from?

cards.text: Then a memory: 'I roused you under the apple tree,' the same spot where that one's mother gave birth. Talk about a family landmark, friend.
Then a big request: "Set me as a seal over your heart, as a seal upon your arm." As a cookie stamper, I have to say it. I RESPECT anybody who wants to leave a mark.

cards.question: The request is to be set as a seal over the heart. What reason does the song give right after it?

answers.text: Love is as strong as death

cards.text: And this love is no little flicker. Its jealousy is as unrelenting as Sheol, and its sparks are fiery flames, and friend, I work next to ovens ALL DAY and even I'm taking a step back.

cards.question: Love's sparks are fiery flames. True or false: the song calls them the fiercest blaze of all.
Love burns that hot. So what can mighty waters do to it?

answers.text: They put it out in time

cards.text: Rivers can't sweep it away either, and then the song asks about money: what if a man gave all the wealth of his house for love? Somebody once bought ME for a quarter at a closing sale, so I am VERY invested in this answer.

cards.question: If a man gave all the wealth of his house for love, his offer would be utterly ___.

cards.text: Then the song shifts: "We have a little sister," and she isn't grown yet. I've got six little ones of my own, friend, so you KNOW I'm leaning in.

cards.question: The speakers have a little sister who isn't grown yet. What are they wondering about her?

answers.text: What to do for her when she is spoken for
How to keep her at home for good
Who should teach her the old songs

cards.question: Here's their plan for the little sister: "If she is a ___, we will build a tower of silver upon her. If she is a ___, we will enclose her with panels of cedar."

cards.text: Then a woman speaks up: "I am a wall," and she says she's grown now, like towers. That is a WHOLE lot of confidence, friend, and I love it.

cards.question: The woman says she is a wall. So what has she become in his eyes?

answers.text: Like one who is far away

cards.text: Solomon, king of Israel, had a vineyard in Baal-hamon, and each tenant had to bring a thousand shekels of silver for its fruit. My rent in the junk drawer was free, and friend, I STILL overpaid.

cards.question: Solomon's vineyard is leased out. Then the speaker talks about another one: "But my own vineyard is mine to ___."
True or false: the speaker says the thousand shekels are for Solomon.

cards.text: And two hundred go to those who tend its fruit. Then a call goes out: "You who dwell in the gardens, my companions are listening for your voice."

cards.question: The companions are listening for the voice of the one in the gardens. True or false: the speaker wants to hear that voice too.

cards.text: And here it is, friend, the very last line of the whole Song of Solomon: "Come away, my beloved." No fireworks, no big finale, just an invitation, and believe me, I know what a good invitation can do.

cards.question: "Come away, my beloved." The beloved is asked to be like what on the mountains of spices?

answers.text: A gazelle or a young stag

findings.problem: Stop 2, card 3 quotes "If she is a ___, we will build a tower of silver upon her. If she is a ___, we will enclose her with panels of cedar.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: Stop 2, card 7 quotes "But my own vineyard is mine to ___.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The card says the two lovers have spent the whole song praising each other. That is a Bible fact from outside the passage, but the card gives no reference for it and cites only Song of Solomon 8:5.

rule.text: Every fact and every verse number comes from that text. Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: Card 6 tells the baker that love's sparks are fiery flames. This true/false card then asks whether the line goes on to say 'the fiercest blaze of all.' That tests the next words of the line, which the baker has no way to reason out.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: This two-blank card asks the baker to supply 'wall' and 'door.' No earlier card sets up the brothers' plan, so the baker can only guess wording they haven't seen. It tests unseen wording rather than meaning, and it makes the pick a matter of luck.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The card introduces Solomon as 'king of Israel,' which comes from outside the passage, but gives no reference for it. The card cites only Song of Solomon 8:11.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: This story card is a plain retelling plus a quote. It has none of Papa Dorin's voice, so it reads stripped down.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The card says the little sister 'isn't grown yet,' which paraphrases a line about her body (8:8), and follows it right away with 'you KNOW I'm leaning in.' Placed there, the joke can read as innuendo.

rule.text: No cursing, crude humor, innuendo, or social or political commentary.

findings.problem: The joke 'That is a WHOLE lot of confidence' reacts to the woman comparing her breasts to towers (8:10). The joke is about her description of her body.

rule.text: Never puts down any person or group: no jokes about age, gender, race, nationality, accents, appearance, intelligence or church denomination.

findings.problem: The joke 'Talk about a family landmark, friend.' is mild and pleasant rather than a real laugh.

rule.text: When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: The card quotes 'I roused you under the apple tree' without saying who speaks. The Song of Solomon text doesn't name the speaker of 8:5b or 8:12 ('my own vineyard').
findings.question: papa-dorin.md says that when he quotes someone speaking as 'I,' he says who it is first. It also says to leave open what the text leaves open. When a poetry passage never names its speaker, as in the Song of Solomon, should Papa Dorin name a likely speaker, use a neutral phrase like 'a voice' or 'the speaker,' or skip naming anyone?
